newsitem.title: GERMANY: Economic impact of French truckers' strike mounts.
newsitem.headline: Economic impact of French truckers' strike mounts.

text.p: The economic impact of the French truckers' strike mounted Thursday as thousands of drivers from across Europe remained stranded despite efforts by Paris to end the labour action.
Drivers from Britain, Spain, Germany and elsewhere endured long queues to cross borders or board ferries as volunteers distributed free sandwiches and coffee in the wintry weather.
The strike has cost European farmers and haulers tens of millions of dollars a day. The timing of the strike, in the commercially crucial pre-Christmas season, could not be worse.

Karl Heinz Schmidt, managing director of the German Transport Association, said 1,000 German trucks were stuck in France, costing hauliers one million marks ($650,000) a day. The indirect impact on German industry would be many times that, he said.
"Starting next week, consumers will see themselves that things like oranges, cauliflowers and Christmas trees will be more expensive," Schmidt told Reuters.
The impact on the car industry could worsen if makers such as Volkswagen AG have to cut back production for lack of parts from suppliers in France and Spain, he said.

At least 1,000 British trucks are also stranded by the strike. "British drivers are being held hostage. It contravenes all principles of the single market and all decency," said Freight Transport Association spokesman Adam Wurf.

The strike may cost Britain five million pounds ($8.4 million) as consequential losses, including drivers' daily salaries, overtime, and costs of diverting vehicles via longer routes, are estimated at 450 pounds ($750) per vehicle per day, Wurf said.
The Spanish Association of International Road Transport said 12,000 to 14,000 Spanish trucks were affected, as France is Spain's only land bridge to the rest of the world.

"November and December are the months in which transport companies make their money," association leader Eduardo Mendez told Reuters. The impact is five times worse than if the strike had taken place in January, he said.
The Spanish Agriculture Ministry estimated losses to the farm sector at some $16 million a day, but said more accurate figures will only become available after the event.
The strike also paralysed Portugal's road transport fleet, which ships tons of fruit and vegetables daily.

Carlos Cazenave, secretary-general of the National Association for the Transport of Goods by Road, told Reuters the total daily cost of the stoppage for the 1,500 Portuguese trucks now stranded in France -- a third of the national fleet -- was about 75 million escudos ($500,000).
He said about 90 percent of Portugal's total fleet was paralysed, with up to 3,000 trucks stuck in Portugal, unable to transport produce to Europe because they cannot cross France.
Portugal's biggest car manufacturing plant, the Ford-Volkswagen AutoEuropa joint venture, was considering halting production outright from Friday if the strike went on.
Belgian ports were clogged by lorries forced to detour from Calais, with massive queues developing and lengthy waiting times to board ferries bound for Britain.
Dutch hauliers organisation EVO said Dutch exporters were losing three to four million guilders a day ($1.7-2.3 million) or some 60 million guilders ($34.9 million) to date due to the road blocks.
The EVO has asked the government to provide financial compensation for the businesses hit hardest, as most insurance policies do not cover losses from this type of protest action.
Swedish vehicle maker AB Volvo said it expected difficulties maintaining production next week if truckers' strikes in France and Denmark continue.
